old_line: \qquad Single-cell RNA-seq experiments provide a snapshot of a cell's transcriptional activity at a point in time; however, the biological differences in a dataset can be overshadowed by technical differences between experimental samples. Laboratory conditions, reagent lots, personnel and instruments introduce technical variation, which becomes a confounder when it is correlated with the biological outcome \citep{leek2010tackling,yu2024assessing}. In single-cell RNA-seq, separately processed technical replicates can differ substantially \citep{tung2017batch}, and single-cell data bring new challenges for modelling batch effects \citep{goh2022batch}. This has led to a variety of batch correction methods, among them Harmony \citep{korsunsky2019fast}, Scanorama \citep{hie2019efficient}, scVI (single-cell variational inference) \citep{lopez2018deep}, its label-aware extension scANVI \citep{xu2021probabilistic} and sysVI \citep{hrovatin2025integrating}. A central challenge of these methods is to balance the alignment of batches with the preservation of biological signal \citep{luecken2022benchmarking}. Under-correction results in datasets that retain substantial batch effects, while over-correction discards key biological information \citep{yu2024assessing}.
new: \qquad Single-cell RNA-seq captures each cell's transcriptional state at one time point, but biological differences in a dataset can be masked by technical differences between samples. Laboratory conditions, reagent lots, personnel and instruments introduce technical variation, which becomes a confounder when it is correlated with the biological outcome \citep{leek2010tackling,yu2024assessing}. Separately processed technical replicates of single-cell RNA-seq can differ substantially \citep{tung2017batch}, and single-cell data pose new problems for modelling batch effects \citep{goh2022batch}. Batch correction methods include Harmony \citep{korsunsky2019fast}, Scanorama \citep{hie2019efficient}, scVI (single-cell variational inference) \citep{lopez2018deep}, its label-aware extension scANVI \citep{xu2021probabilistic} and sysVI \citep{hrovatin2025integrating}. Each must balance the alignment of batches against the preservation of biological signal \citep{luecken2022benchmarking}: under-correction leaves substantial batch effects, and over-correction discards biological information \citep{yu2024assessing}.

old_line: \qquad With the adoption of deep learning-based methods in single-cell analysis, techniques for trainable end-to-end batch correction are necessary. A notable class of deep-learning approaches, latent-variable models, aim to learn a low-dimensional representation of the RNA-seq readout that captures salient signals corresponding to biological programs. To align these latent spaces across batches, two primary methods have been adopted: decoder conditioning, which passes the batch label as an input variable to the decoder responsible for reconstructing the input RNA-seq vector from the latent variable \citep{lopez2018deep}, and adversarial batch, which trains a network to predict the batch, or another confounder such as age, from each cell's latent code and penalizes the encoder whenever that prediction succeeds  \citep{ganin2016domain,dincer2020adversarial}.
new: \qquad Deep-learning methods for single-cell analysis need batch correction that is trained end to end with the model. Latent-variable models learn a low-dimensional representation of the RNA-seq readout that captures biological programs. Two approaches align these latent spaces across batches: decoder conditioning, which passes the batch label to the decoder that reconstructs the input RNA-seq vector from the latent variable \citep{lopez2018deep}, and adversarial training, which trains a network to predict the batch, or another confounder such as age, from each cell's latent code and penalizes the encoder whenever that prediction succeeds \citep{ganin2016domain,dincer2020adversarial}.

old_line: \qquad Adversarial methods are split between discriminator approaches, which minimize the Jensen--Shannon (JS) divergence \citep{goodfellow2014generative} between samples from different batches or confounding variables \citep{ganin2016domain,dincer2020adversarial}, and Wasserstein critic-based methods, which minimize the Wasserstein-1 (W1) distance \citep{arjovsky2017wasserstein,gulrajani2017improved} between such samples. These techniques have been applied extensively to single-cell batch correction.
new: \qquad Adversarial methods use either a discriminator, which minimizes the Jensen--Shannon (JS) divergence \citep{goodfellow2014generative} between samples from different batches or confounder values \citep{ganin2016domain,dincer2020adversarial}, or a Wasserstein critic, which minimizes the Wasserstein-1 (W1) distance \citep{arjovsky2017wasserstein,gulrajani2017improved} between such samples. Both have been applied widely to single-cell batch correction.

old_line: \qquad iMAP trained a critic with the gradient penalty of the Wasserstein generative adversarial network (WGAN-GP), correcting every dataset towards one anchor dataset that is left unchanged \citep{wang2021imap}. iDLC trains a WGAN-GP critic, with a Sinkhorn transport term added to the generator loss, to map each source batch onto a reference batch \citep{jiang2026geometric}; scStarCorrect also aligns every batch to one fixed reference batch, but through a domain-aware discriminator whose loss form its abstract does not state \citep{gu2025scstarcorrect}; Beaconet trains one Wasserstein critic per batch against the mixture of the other batches and needs no reference \citep{xu2024beaconet}. IMGG trains a WGAN-GP generator towards a synthetic intermediate batch built from cells matched across batches \citep{wang2022imgg}, ResPAN combines a Wasserstein GAN with random-walk mutual-nearest-neighbour pairing \citep{wang2022respan}, and IMAAE uses a loss of WGAN-GP form, an anchor batch and known cell labels \citep{wang2023integrating}. Methods built on a standard discriminator are numerous as well. Portal trains two logistic discriminators and clamps their logits so that cells scored as clearly dataset-specific give no gradient and are not forced to mix \citep{zhao2022adversarial}; AIF pairs a real-versus-reconstructed discriminator with a batch classifier that the encoder is trained against \citep{monnier2024novel}; and ABC trains an autoencoder against a multi-class batch discriminator alongside cell-type classifier branches that use labels \citep{danino2024batch}.

old_line: \qquad A third route avoids training an adversary network altogether by measuring the distance between the latent batches explicitly. These include the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) \citep{gretton2012kernel}, and optimal transport (OT) measures \citep{cuturi2013sinkhorn, genevay2018learning,feydy2019interpolating}. A full mathematical formulation of these approaches is available in \replaced{Supplementary Note 1}{supplementary note XXX}. Both measures have been used to align single-cell batches without an adversary. MMD-ResNet trains a residual network to match the distribution of one batch to that of another \citep{shaham2017removal}, SAUCIE applies an MMD penalty against a reference batch on an internal layer \citep{amodio2019exploring}, trVAE places an MMD term across conditions in the first decoder layer \citep{lotfollahi2020conditional}, uniPort couples a variational autoencoder with minibatch unbalanced OT \citep{cao2022unified}, and Li et al.\ added an MMD term between batches to the loss of an early scVI version \citep{li2022trade}.
new: \qquad A third route measures the distance between the latent batches directly, with no adversary network: the maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) \citep{gretton2012kernel} and optimal transport (OT) measures \citep{cuturi2013sinkhorn, genevay2018learning,feydy2019interpolating} (formulations in Supplementary Note 1). Both have been used to align single-cell batches. MMD-ResNet trains a residual network to match the distribution of one batch to that of another \citep{shaham2017removal}, SAUCIE applies an MMD penalty against a reference batch on an internal layer \citep{amodio2019exploring}, trVAE places an MMD term across conditions in the first decoder layer \citep{lotfollahi2020conditional}, uniPort couples a variational autoencoder with minibatch unbalanced OT \citep{cao2022unified}, and Li et al.\ added an MMD term between batches to the loss of an early scVI version \citep{li2022trade}.

old_line: \qquad Despite their promise, \replaced{alignment penalties}{adversarial methods} have limitations that challenge their utility in practice. When batches contain different cell-type proportions, a lower bound on classification error grows as the latent distributions of the two batches are aligned more tightly \citep{zhao2019learning}, and exact alignment under any divergence that is zero only for identical distributions leaves an error at least as large as the proportion gap \citep{wu2019domain}. The sysVI study found that an adversarial conditional variational autoencoder and an adversarial multi-omics integration method mixed unrelated cell types when proportions were unbalanced across batches, and more so at higher adversarial strength \citep{hrovatin2025integrating}; dataset imbalance also changed clustering, annotation, differential expression, query mapping and trajectories across five integration methods \citep{maan2024characterizing}.
new: \qquad Alignment penalties have known limits. When batches contain different cell-type proportions, a lower bound on classification error grows as the latent distributions of the two batches are aligned more tightly \citep{zhao2019learning}, and exact alignment under any divergence that is zero only for identical distributions leaves an error at least as large as the proportion gap \citep{wu2019domain}. new: \qquad Each method adds a penalty, weighted by a fixed strength, to the scVI loss (Table~\ref{tab:1}). old_line: \qquad We benchmark these methods on eight integration tasks of the single-cell integration benchmark (scIB) \citep{luecken2022benchmarking}, used as distributed with their batch and cell-type labels. These consist of six real datasets from different biological settings, four of single-cell RNA sequencing (human pancreas, lung, immune cells, and joint human--mouse immune cells) and two of chromatin accessibility (\added{assay for transposase-accessible chromatin, }ATAC; mouse brain, a small and a large dataset, as gene-activity matrices), and two simulated datasets. RNA tasks use 2,000 highly variable genes and the ATAC tasks all features; counts are used as distributed. The full details of the datasets are available in Supplementary Table S1. We score each method using the scIB batch, biology, and aggregate selection scores. The batch score is the mean of five metrics: principal-component regression on batch, batch average silhouette width (ASW), graph integration local inverse Simpson's index (iLISI), graph connectivity and the k-nearest-neighbor batch-effect test (kBET). The biology score is the mean of the task's biology metrics: normalized mutual information and adjusted Rand index between clusters and cell-type labels, cell-type ASW, isolated-label F1, isolated-label silhouette, graph cell-type LISI (cLISI), plus cell-cycle conservation on the four real RNA tasks and trajectory conservation on the two immune tasks, which have pseudotime. The mathematical formulation of these metrics is available in Supplementary Note 3. The scIB combined selection score is the weighted average $0.4\,\mathrm{batch} + 0.6\,\mathrm{biology}$\added{.}

Its strengths and $b^*$ were set from the sweep's batch scores after the sweep had been read, so it replicates the sweep's readings rather than testing a hypothesis fixed before the sweep.
